prerequisites: A diploid organism has two alleles at a locus.
Genotype names the alleles; phenotype is the observable trait.

lesson.title: Rebuild the idea step by step
lesson.keyIdea: One dominant allele can be enough to produce the dominant phenotype under complete dominance.
lesson.workedExample: In a synthetic plant, C gives curled leaves and c gives flat leaves with complete dominance. CC and Cc both have curled leaves; only cc has flat leaves. The c allele is still present in Cc even though its effect is masked.
steps: Write the two alleles in each possible genotype.
Use the stated dominance rule to predict each phenotype.
Work backward from the observed phenotype; keep every genotype that fits.

probes.prompt: Could a Pp plant have purple flowers under complete dominance? State what each allele contributes to your prediction.
In a Pp plant, does the p allele remain present when the dominant trait is visible? Explain what you mean by “dominant”.
Could a Rr plant have red flowers under complete dominance? State what each allele contributes to your prediction.
In a Rr plant, does the r allele remain present when the dominant trait is visible? Explain what you mean by “dominant”.

prerequisites: A gamete receives one allele per locus.
Fertilization combines one gamete from each parent.

lesson.title: Rebuild the idea step by step
lesson.keyIdea: Separate alleles into gametes before combining parental possibilities.
lesson.workedExample: For a synthetic one-locus cross Dd × dd with complete dominance and equal gamete probabilities, the first parent contributes D or d with probability 1/2 each. The second contributes d only. Offspring are Dd or dd with probability 1/2 each. These are probabilities, not a guarantee of exact counts in a small family.
steps: List the possible gametes for each parent, one allele per gamete.
Combine one gamete from each parent and multiply their probabilities.
Group identical genotypes; translate to phenotypes only if asked.

probes.prompt: Focus only on a Tt parent. Which allele or alleles can one gamete carry at this locus? Explain how the parent produces those gametes.
For Tt × Tt, list the possible gametes from each parent separately. Then show how one pair of gametes forms one offspring genotype; are you counting genotypes or visible traits?
Focus only on a Bb parent. Which allele or alleles can one gamete carry at this locus? Explain how the parent produces those gametes.
For Bb × bb, list the possible gametes from each parent separately. Then show how one pair of gametes forms one offspring genotype; are you counting genotypes or visible traits?

prerequisites: Each gamete gets one allele from each locus.
For unlinked genes in this model, allele choices at different loci are independent.

lesson.title: Rebuild the idea step by step
lesson.keyIdea: Choose one allele per locus, then combine independent choices.
lesson.workedExample: For a synthetic EeFf parent with unlinked genes and equal segregation, E or e each has probability 1/2, independently of F or f. EF, Ef, eF and ef therefore each have probability 1/4. In EeFf × eeff, the other parent contributes ef only, giving four equally likely offspring genotypes. Complete dominance translates these into four phenotypes.
steps: List the allele options at the first locus.
Pair each with every option at the second unlinked locus.
Multiply independent probabilities, then combine with the other parent’s actual gametes.

probes.prompt: For the AaBb parent, the two genes are unlinked. After a gamete receives A, must it also receive B, or could it receive b? Explain why.
How many alleles should one gamete from AaBb contain at each of these two loci? List all combinations by pairing one choice at each locus and explain their probabilities.
For the RrYy parent, the two genes are unlinked. After a gamete receives R, must it also receive Y, or could it receive y? Explain why.
How many alleles should one gamete from RrYy contain at each of these two loci? List all combinations by pairing one choice at each locus and explain their probabilities.
